list.name: namespace
list.label: Instance
list.description: The instance this board reads. Empty on purpose: the chart's templates/grafana-dashboard.yaml replaces this entry with a hidden constant naming the instance it installs, so every namespace="$namespace" selector reads that instance's series and no other. There is no instance picker: each instance ships its own copy of this board, in its own Grafana folder.

list.name: instance
list.label: Instance ID
list.description: The instance ID, used to select this instance's alerts. Empty on purpose: the chart's templates/grafana-dashboard.yaml replaces this entry with a hidden constant holding the ID of the instance it installs.

title: DeviceChain — Platform
description: Platform board: whether the instance's workloads are healthy (replicas, restarts, memory and CPU against their requests and limits), how each service's runtime is behaving, sign-in and single sign-on, tenant deletion progress, per-tenant ceilings and safety gates, and the opt-in AI inference service. Each instance gets its own copy of this board, scoped to it; there is no instance picker. Charts for opt-in services stay empty until the service is installed.

panels.title: Firing alerts
panels.description: Alerts firing right now for this instance that concern command delivery. An empty table means none are firing. Alerts come from the instance's Prometheus rules, so the table stays empty if those rules are not installed.

panels.title: Replicas missing
panels.description: Replicas the instance's workloads want that are not available right now, summed over all workloads. Zero is healthy. When it is above zero, find the workload on the chart below, then look at its pods for a failing start, a missing image or a node with no room.

panels.title: Pods not ready
panels.description: Pods in the instance that exist but are not passing their readiness check. A pod that is slowly starting shows here briefly; one that stays here is not serving. Describe the pod to see which check is failing.

panels.title: Container restarts in range
panels.description: Times a container restarted during the selected time range. One restart is worth a look: a service ends itself on purpose when it cannot do its job, and Kubernetes starts it again within seconds. Read the previous container's log for the reason.

panels.title: Containers last stopped for lack of memory
panels.description: Containers whose most recent stop was the system killing them for exceeding their memory limit. It stays at 1 until the container stops again for another reason. Raise the memory limit or find what grew; the memory charts below show the climb.

panels.title: Replicas available against wanted
panels.description: For each workload, the replicas the instance wants and the replicas that are available. The two lines should sit together. A gap means a rollout in progress or pods that cannot start.

panels.title: Container restarts
panels.description: Restarts per container as they happen. Several containers restarting together usually points at something they share, such as the message broker or the database, rather than at each service.

panels.title: Memory in use against limit
panels.description: Working memory of each container as a fraction of its memory limit. Near 100% the container will be killed. Containers with no limit set do not appear. A line that climbs steadily under steady load means memory is leaking: restart it for now and report it.

targets.expr: sum by (pod, container) (container_memory_working_set_bytes{namespace="$namespace", container!="", container!="POD"}) / sum by (pod, container) (kube_pod_container_resource_limits{namespace="$namespace", resource="memory"})

panels.title: Memory in use
panels.description: Working memory of each pod, in bytes. Compare it with the memory request and limit set for the instance; a pod that keeps growing needs a larger limit or has a leak.

panels.title: CPU use against request
panels.description: CPU time each container is using as a fraction of the CPU it asked for. Above 100% is allowed when the node has room, but a container that stays far above its request is competing for CPU and the request should be raised. Containers with no request set do not appear.

targets.expr: sum by (pod, container) (rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{namespace="$namespace", container!="", container!="POD"}[$__rate_interval])) / sum by (pod, container) (kube_pod_container_resource_requests{namespace="$namespace", resource="cpu"})

panels.title: CPU throttling
panels.description: Fraction of scheduling periods in which a container was held back because it hit its CPU limit. Anything steadily above a few percent slows that service down even when the node is idle. Raise the CPU limit or remove it.

targets.expr: sum by (pod) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total{namespace="$namespace", container!="", container!="POD"}[$__rate_interval])) / sum by (pod) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total{namespace="$namespace", container!="", container!="POD"}[$__rate_interval]))

panels.title: Goroutines
panels.description: Concurrent tasks running inside each service. Steady under steady load is healthy. A count that only climbs means tasks are piling up, which usually follows a slow or unreachable dependency. The highest replica of each service is drawn.

panels.title: Heap in use
panels.description: Memory the service's own code is holding for live data. Rising with load and falling back is normal; rising and never falling back is a leak. Compare with the container memory chart above.

panels.title: Memory resident in the process
panels.description: Memory the operating system has given each service process. It runs above the heap figure because it also holds stacks and runtime overhead. The highest replica of each service is drawn.

panels.title: Garbage collection runs
panels.description: How often each service reclaims memory. A rate that keeps rising with no more load means the service is allocating faster than it should and is spending CPU on cleanup.

panels.title: Longest recent garbage collection pause
panels.description: The longest pause a service took for memory cleanup in its recent runs. Pauses above a few tens of milliseconds delay message handling. Look for large heap growth at the same time.

panels.title: Open file handles against limit
panels.description: Open files and network connections as a fraction of what each service process may open. Near 100% the service refuses new connections. A steady climb points at connections that are never closed.

panels.title: Sign-in checks refused for capacity (range)
panels.description: Password and client-secret checks that failed because the attempt store was unreachable or full, or one request used up its check budget, over the selected range. These are refusals by the platform, not wrong passwords. Check user-management's health and its attempt store.

panels.title: Throttled sign-in attempts (range)
panels.description: Attempts held back because the account has had too many recent failures. A few are normal after a person mistypes. A steady count against one account suggests password guessing.

panels.title: Single sign-on refusals (range)
panels.description: Single sign-on attempts refused after the identity provider vouched for the person, over the selected range: unverified email or domain, a required claim missing, or an identity that may not hold a system role. Each one needs a person to review the identity provider's configuration.

panels.title: Identity provider fetch failures (range)
panels.description: Times user-management could not reach a configured identity provider to complete single sign-on, over the selected range. Check the provider's address and certificate and the instance's outbound network access.

panels.title: Password and client-secret checks by outcome
panels.description: Every credential check, split by result. Mostly success is healthy. Rising throttled, unavailable, store_full or request_budget needs attention: see the tiles above.

panels.title: Single sign-on attempts by outcome
panels.description: Every single sign-on attempt, split by result. Nothing here until single sign-on is configured. Anything other than success is a person who could not sign in; the outcome name says why.

panels.title: Identity provider fetch failures by connection
panels.description: Failed contact with each single sign-on connection's identity provider. Nothing here until single sign-on is configured. Look at the connection named in the legend.

panels.title: Token key fetches by service
panels.description: Each service regularly fetches the keys that sign access tokens from user-management. Failures mean that service may stop verifying tokens. Failures that persist point at user-management or the network between them.

panels.title: Deletions in progress
panels.description: Tenants whose data is being erased right now. Zero most of the time. Only the replica holding the coordinator's lease reports, so a standby reads zero and the highest value is shown.

panels.title: Oldest open deletion
panels.description: Age of the longest-running tenant deletion. A deletion normally waits out a hold period before it completes; one open for much longer than that is stuck. Look at the stores holding it back below.

panels.title: Deletions completed (range)
panels.description: Tenant deletions that finished during the selected range: every store clean and the tenant name released.

panels.title: Deletion attempts that failed (range)
panels.description: Passes in which the coordinator could not carry a deletion forward, over the selected range. The pass is retried, so a brief count is harmless. A count that keeps growing needs the user-management log.

panels.title: Stores holding back a deletion
panels.description: Storage systems that have not yet confirmed a deleted tenant's data is gone. deferred means the store reports the data still present or arriving, which clears by itself; error means it could not be asked, which needs attention.

panels.title: Rows erased by store
panels.description: Records, files, messages or keys erased per second for deleted tenants, by storage system. This is the sign a held-back store is making progress.

panels.title: Erase call time by store
panels.description: 95th percentile time one storage system took to answer an erase request. Slow answers from one store delay every deletion that includes it.

panels.title: Safety gates switched off
panels.description: Optional protections that are not active in a running service because their setting is absent, so work they exist to refuse gets through. Zero is healthy. The tiles below name each gate.

panels.title: Tenants metered at the platform default (range)
panels.description: Admissions where a service could not read a tenant's own ceiling and used the platform default instead, over the selected range. A tenant on a lower ceiling is admitted more than it should be. Check user-management's health.

panels.title: Shared allowance in use (range)
panels.description: Admissions that fell into the one allowance shared by unconfirmed tenant names, over the selected range. Usually something is posting to many invented tenant names on the HTTP ingest port.

panels.title: Outbound actions shed (range)
panels.description: Outbound calls dropped because a tenant exceeded its outbound ceiling, over the selected range. Find the tenant with dead letters of reason shed and raise its ceiling if the traffic is legitimate.

panels.title: Safety gates
panels.description: Each optional protection and whether it is on. OFF means the gate's setting is absent in that service and the work it guards is not being refused.

panels.title: Ceilings hit by device traffic
panels.description: Device messages and readings turned away because a tenant sent faster than its ceiling, by ingest source. Short bursts are the limiter doing its job. A tenant that stays limited needs a higher ceiling or a quieter fleet.

panels.title: Ceilings hit by outbound calls
panels.description: Outbound calls shed for being over a tenant's outbound ceiling, by action, as seen by the rules engine and by the connector sender. The two should agree; calls refused at the sender but not at the rules engine mean the two are configured with different ceilings.

panels.title: Admissions metered without the tenant's ceiling
panels.description: Admissions by dimension and cause where the tenant's own ceiling was not available. cause=unreachable means user-management could not be asked; cause=unknown-tenant is traffic for a name the platform does not know.

panels.title: Inference calls by outcome
panels.description: Requests to draft a detection rule from plain language, by result. Nothing here unless the opt-in AI inference service is installed and a tenant uses it. rate_limited means a tenant hit its inference ceiling; consent_required means it has not opted in to an external model; provider_error means the model provider failed.

panels.title: Model tokens used
panels.description: Tokens sent to and received from the model provider, per second. Nothing here unless the opt-in AI inference service is installed. This is the figure the provider bills on.
